lesson.title: The False Alarm: Understanding Type I Error
lesson.summary: A Type I error happens when you reject a null hypothesis that is actually true, a false alarm, and its probability is controlled directly by the significance level you chose.
lesson.body:
A Type I error occurs when a test rejects H0 even though H0 is actually true. It is a false positive: the data looked convincing enough to trigger significance, but there was, in fact, no real effect or difference, and ordinary sampling variability alone produced a misleadingly extreme result. Because rejecting H0 happens exactly when p is less than alpha, and alpha is the pre-set tolerance for how often you are willing to be fooled by chance, it follows that if H0 really is true, the probability of committing a Type I error is exactly alpha. That is exactly why alpha is called the significance level, it is a chosen tolerance for how often this specific kind of false alarm is allowed to happen.

A classic way to picture this is a courtroom, with H0 standing for "the defendant is innocent." A Type I error is convicting an innocent person: the evidence presented was convincing enough to clear the "beyond a reasonable doubt" bar, but the defendant genuinely did not commit the crime.

Ground this in the cereal box test. H0: mu = 16 was rejected at alpha = 0.05 because p = 0.0456 is less than 0.05. Now suppose, hypothetically, that the machine actually is perfectly calibrated at 16 ounces, and that particular sample of 36 boxes with a mean of 15.9 was simply an unusually light draw, the kind of draw that happens with roughly the probability captured by the p-value even when nothing is wrong. In that case, rejecting H0 would be a Type I error. Because alpha was set to 0.05 before the data were collected, this kind of false alarm would happen at most about 5 percent of the time in the long run, if H0 really is true and the test were repeated over and over with fresh samples.

Here is the key limitation to keep in mind: you can never know, for any single test, whether you actually made a Type I error, because you never observe the true population parameter directly, that is the entire reason a test was needed in the first place. All you can control in advance is the long-run rate at which this kind of error would occur if H0 were true, and that control happens through the choice of alpha.
